chunks: verily Divine orders descend from heaven to earth like drops of rain, bringing to every one what is destined for him whether plenty or paucity.
So if any one of you observes for his brother plenty of progeny or of wealth or of self, it should not be a worry for him.
So long as a Muslim does not commit such an act that if it is disclosed he has to bend his eyes (in shame) and by which low people are emboldened,
he is like the gambler who expects that the first draw of his arrow would secure him gain and also cover up the previous loss.
ai.seo_question: What is the Islamic perspective on envy and contentment with divine decree?
ai.summary: Imam Ali employs the metaphor of a gambler awaiting a winning draw to illustrate how hidden moral flaws (dana'ah) can become sources of public shame and social temptation, urging believers to maintain inner dignity. This teaching, central to the chapter on contentment, emphasizes that true piety involves guarding against the 'fitna' (trial/distraction) of comparing one's divine portion with others' abundance. It reflects the Shia emphasis on internal spiritual integrity over external worldly status.
